edition: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, version 1.10; PDF Published Time 2023-11-14T15:20:08Z; 13 pages
coverage: All 200 lines / 13 pages; sections 4.1-4.6; Figures 4.1-4.5 and the xv6 struct listing; asides on time/space sharing, policy/mechanism separation, the process list, and key terms; references and simulation homework; raster figures not visually inspected
sections: 4.3 Process Creation: A Little More Detail
figures: Figure 4.1: Loading: From Program To Process
Figure 4.2: Process: State Transitions
Figure 4.3: Tracing Process State: CPU Only
Figure 4.4: Tracing Process State: CPU and I/O
Figure 4.5: The xv6 Proc Structure
notes: Source claim: a process is a running program, and the OS creates the illusion of many CPUs by time sharing one or a few physical CPUs; the stated cost is slower per-process progress while the CPU is shared.
Source claim: a process's machine state is an inventory of its address space, registers (including the program counter and stack pointer), and I/O state such as open files.
Source claim: any process API needs create, destroy, wait, miscellaneous control (suspend/resume), and status operations; the chapter presents these as generic rather than UNIX-specific.

Source claim: creation loads code and static data, allocates and initializes the stack with argc/argv, may allocate a heap, sets up standard file descriptors, and then jumps to main(); loading may be eager or lazy.

Source claim: the simplified states are running, ready, and blocked, with scheduled/descheduled and I/O initiate/complete transitions; xv6 adds unused, embryonic, sleeping, runnable, and zombie states.

Source claim: xv6's struct proc stores memory bounds, kernel stack, state, pid, parent, sleep channel, open files, cwd, saved register context, and trap frame; a context switch saves and restores that register context.
Source claim: a zombie has exited but not been reaped; the parent's wait() retrieves the exit status and releases the remaining process structures.

Inference: the chapter bundles scheduling identity, address space, and I/O ownership into one abstraction; later thread and container designs deliberately separate some of these, which the chapter does not examine.
Inference: the policy/mechanism split is presented as modularity, but the chapter gives no cost model for switching frequency or policy choice, so the performance consequences remain qualitative.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Process and task lifecycle vocabulary: running, ready, blocked, and ownership of waiting; compare OS process states with the book's task states.
Diagnostic distinction between runnable and blocked work, PID-level identity, and CPU-time attribution.
Time sharing versus space sharing as competing demand models for a finite resource; useful analogy for capacity sharing.

notes: Source claim: fork() creates a nearly exact copy with a private address space, registers, and PC; the parent receives the child PID, the child receives zero, and failure returns a negative value.
Source claim: after fork() either process may run first; output order is non-deterministic because the CPU scheduler decides, so programs should not rely on it.
Source claim: wait() blocks the parent until the child exits, making the example output deterministic; a footnote concedes that wait() can return before child exit in some cases.
Source claim: exec() replaces the calling program's code and static data, reinitializes the heap and stack, keeps the same process, and does not return on success; Linux exposes six variants.
Source claim: the shell exploits the fork/exec gap to redirect output by closing STDOUT_FILENO and opening a file; UNIX allocates the lowest free descriptor, and descriptors survive exec().
Source claim: pipes use an in-kernel queue to connect one process's output to another's input, enabling command pipelines such as grep | wc.

Source claim: kill() and signals (for example SIGINT from control-c and SIGTSTP from control-z) control processes and process groups; ownership limits control to a user's own processes, with the superuser exempt.
Source claim: the authors cite [B+19] as arguing that fork() has design problems and advocating spawn()-style creation, and they explicitly present their positive view as an opinion.
Inference: the fork/exec split buys flexibility (redirection, pipes, environment changes) at the cost of a two-process mental model and failure paths that the short examples do not exercise.
Inference: the chapter describes fork() as giving each process its own memory but does not discuss copy-on-write or fork failure under memory pressure, so implementation cost is out of scope.

tycho_candidates.candidate: API design trade-off between one flexible primitive and a smaller, safer operation; fork's asymmetric return contract is a clarity example.
Separation of launching work from configuring and executing it; cancellation and signal-like control surfaces.
Principal-scoped control: users may signal only their own processes, with a privileged override; maps to authorization boundaries.

unit: Complete chapter 6, Mechanism: Limited Direct Execution
edition: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, version 1.10; PDF Published Time 2023-11-14T15:20:46Z; 16 pages
coverage: All 377 lines / 16 pages; sections 6.1-6.5 plus the opening crux box, chapter summary and references; figures 6.1-6.4 (direct-execution protocol, limited-direct-execution protocol, timer-interrupt protocol, xv6 swtch assembly listing); asides and tips on procedure-call disguise, protected control transfer, user inputs in secure systems, application misbehavior, timer interrupt, reboot, context-switch cost, and key CPU-virtualization terms; homework (measurement) prompt and its measurement aside; raster figures not visually inspected
figures: Figure 6.1: Direct Execution Protocol (Without Limits)
Figure 6.2: Limited Direct Execution Protocol
Figure 6.3: Limited Direct Execution Protocol (Timer Interrupt)
Figure 6.4: The xv6 Context Switch Code
notes: [Source] The chapter frames CPU virtualization as a two-constraint problem: direct execution buys performance, while limits buy control, and it states that both hardware and OS support are required (sections 6.1-6.2).

[Source] Two execution modes are the primitive: user mode blocks privileged operations such as I/O and trap-table installation, kernel mode permits them, and the trap instruction is the only sanctioned crossing (section 6.2, tip on protected control transfer).

[Source] Trap dispatch is indirected through a boot-time trap table and a system-call number rather than a user-supplied jump address; the chapter explicitly calls this indirection a form of protection (section 6.2).
[Source] Figure 6.2 decomposes the protocol into boot-time setup (trap table, first timer arming) and per-run transitions, with hardware saving registers onto a per-process kernel stack.

[Source] Cooperative relinquishment through system calls, yield, or faults cannot bound a spinning process; the timer interrupt is presented as the minimal hardware addition that restores OS control without process cooperation (section 6.3).

[Source] The context switch is described as two separate save/restore pairs: implicit hardware saves on trap, then explicit software saves into the process structure inside switch(); changing the kernel stack pointer is what makes return-from-trap resume B instead of A (section 6.3, Figure 6.3).

[Source] The xv6 swtch listing in Figure 6.4 makes the mechanism concrete: the return address is popped into the old context, %esp is stored, then a fresh return address is pushed and ret resumes the new context.

[Source] Section 6.4 concedes that an interrupt during trap handling is a real problem and defers it to the concurrency material, sketching interrupt disabling while flagging lost interrupts as the cost of overusing it.

[Inference] The lmbench figures quoted in the context-switch aside are 1996 hardware measurements plus a qualitative modern remark, so they are not usable as a current latency budget without fresh measurement.

[Inference] The baby-proofing analogy implies a perimeter security posture: once traps and the timer are configured, the kernel still has to distrust the arguments crossing the boundary, which is the residual attack surface the user-input tip names.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Use the user/kernel split as a minimal contrast case: hardware-enforced privilege is a different class of boundary from application-level authorization, which would keep the isolation claims in that chapter scoped.

Mirror the chapter's mechanism-versus-policy split: trap, timer and context switch are mechanisms, while the scheduler is policy, which maps onto separating runtime thread mechanics from executor scheduling choices.
Does task lifetime distinguish an OS context switch from cooperative cancellation and application-level timeouts?

coverage: All 264 lines / 13 pages; sections 7.1-7.10 plus the opening crux box, chapter summary and references; figures 7.1-7.9 (FIFO simple, FIFO convoy, SJF simple, SJF with late arrivals, STCF, SJF for response time, round robin, poor I/O overlap, overlapping I/O); asides and tips on preemptive schedulers, the SJF principle, amortization, and overlap; homework (simulation) with 7 numbered questions; raster figures not visually inspected
figures: Figure 7.1: FIFO Simple Example
Figure 7.2: Why FIFO Is Not That Great
Figure 7.3: SJF Simple Example
Figure 7.4: SJF With Late Arrivals From B and C
Figure 7.5: STCF Simple Example
Figure 7.6: SJF Again (Bad for Response Time)
Figure 7.7: Round Robin (Good For Response Time)
Figure 7.8: Poor Use Of Resources
Figure 7.9: Overlap Allows Better Use Of Resources
notes: [Source] Policy is built by progressively relaxing five stated workload assumptions; the chapter singles out known job runtime as the worst offender because it would make the scheduler omniscient (section 7.1).
[Source] Turnaround time is completion minus arrival, which collapses to completion time under simultaneous arrivals; FIFO averages 110 seconds on the 100/10/10 example (sections 7.2-7.3).
[Source] The convoy effect names FIFO's failure when a long job blocks short ones, and SJF lowers that same example's average turnaround to 50 seconds (sections 7.3-7.4).
[Source] SJF is non-preemptive, so short jobs arriving late still wait; STCF preempts and re-ranks by remaining time on each arrival, reaching 50 seconds in the late-arrival example (section 7.5).

[Source] Response time is first-run minus arrival, the metric under which STCF is poor and round robin strong: 1 second average versus 5 seconds in the three-job, five-second example (sections 7.6-7.7).

[Source] Time-slice length is an explicit trade-off: shorter slices improve response time while context-switch cost, including cache, TLB and branch-predictor state, must be amortized, so the slice cannot shrink without bound (section 7.7, tip on amortization).

[Source] Round robin is called nearly pessimal for turnaround (average 14 seconds in the same example), and the chapter generalizes that any policy fair on a small time scale will trade away turnaround time (section 7.7).

[Source] I/O is folded in by treating each CPU burst as an independent job, so a blocked process yields the CPU and its next burst can preempt a long CPU-bound job, producing overlap and better utilization (section 7.8).

[Inference] The claim that STCF is provably optimal is scoped to the chapter's assumptions and the single turnaround metric; it is not evidence for multicore, multi-metric, or I/O-heavy behavior, which the text does not analyze.

[Inference] The assumption ladder is a reusable audit device: a workload profile could record which assumptions (equal length, known runtime, no I/O, run to completion) are violated and which single metric the design is optimizing.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Distinguish response time from turnaround time explicitly: the chapter shows a policy can be excellent on first-response latency and pessimal on completion time, which would sharpen what a stated latency objective actually measures.

Use the quantum-versus-switch-cost arithmetic (10 ms slice against 1 ms switch, then a 100 ms slice for amortization) as a compact illustration of why pool sizing and yield frequency trade throughput for responsiveness.
Does the measurement page distinguish first-response latency from completion time over a finite observation window?

unit: Complete chapter 8, Scheduling: The Multi-Level Feedback Queue

coverage: All 223 lines / 12 pages; sections 8.1-8.6, References, Homework; figures 8.1-8.6 (queue snapshot, long-running job, two interactive examples, boost on/off, gaming on/off, unequal quanta); four TIP asides; six homework questions; no code listings; raster figures not visually inspected

notes: Source claim: MLFQ originated with Corbato et al.'s 1962 CTSS work and is presented as a way to approximate short-job-first scheduling without knowing job length in advance.
Source claim: Rules 1-2 make priority strict across queues and round-robin within one, while Rules 3-4 move a job down as it consumes its per-level allotment.
Source claim: the first priority-changing design let a job keep its level whenever it yielded before the allotment expired; the chapter identifies this as both a starvation risk and a gaming vector.
Source claim: Rule 5 boosts every job to the top queue after interval S, which bounds starvation and lets a job that became interactive re-enter at high priority.
Source claim: Rule 4 replaces 4a/4b with cumulative accounting, so splitting CPU use across many I/O yields no longer preserves a high queue position.
Source claim: queue parameters are deliberately unequal, with short slices at high priority and long slices at low priority; Solaris TS is cited with 60 queues and roughly one-second boosts.
Source claim: FreeBSD 4.3 used decayed CPU usage rather than explicit queues, and some systems reserve top priorities for kernel work or expose nice as optional advice.

Inference: the anti-gaming property depends on trustworthy per-job CPU accounting at each level; the chapter does not describe how that accounting is implemented, migrated across CPUs, or protected from coarse clock granularity.
Inference: all performance evidence in the chapter is illustrative trace diagrams, so the parameter guidance is experience-based rather than measured in the text.
Representation note: the page footers print VERSION 1.10 and copyright through 2023, consistent with the 2023-11-14 PDF timestamp.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Use MLFQ's feedback-plus-boost pattern as a candidate priority/fairness policy: latency-sensitive classes get preference, but a bounded boost interval must guarantee progress for batch classes.
Noisy-neighbor control needs more than quotas: dynamic priority can starve a long-running tenant, so document anti-starvation boost or reserved-share assumptions.
Separate OS-level time-slice and priority assumptions from application runtime scheduler assumptions; MLFQ's priority changes are not a stable contract an application can rely on.

notes: Source claim: proportional-share scheduling targets a defined fraction of CPU rather than turnaround or response time, and lottery scheduling realizes the fraction probabilistically through tickets.
Source claim: ticket currency, transfer, and inflation are mechanisms for reallocating shares; the chapter warns that inflation is only sensible among processes that trust one another.
Source claim: the lottery implementation draws one random number over the total tickets and walks a list accumulating each job's tickets until the counter passes the winner.
Source claim: sorting the job list by ticket count does not change which job wins but can reduce the expected number of list steps.
Source claim: the chapter's fairness metric is the first completion time divided by the second; simulator results show poor fairness for short jobs and convergence toward 1 as jobs lengthen.
Source claim: stride scheduling uses a stride inversely proportional to tickets and always runs the smallest pass value, giving exact proportions per cycle but requiring global per-job pass state.
Source claim: CFS selects the lowest vruntime, derives slices from sched_latency divided by runnable count, floors them at min_granularity, and maps nice -20..+19 to weights with 1024 at nice 0.
Source claim: CFS scales vruntime accrual by 1024/weight_i and stores runnable jobs in a red-black tree; a waking job's vruntime is set to the tree minimum to prevent a catch-up monopoly.
Source claim: the chapter names Linux 6.6's EEVDF as the current default and concedes that proportional-share schedulers interact poorly with I/O and leave ticket/priority assignment unresolved.
Representation note: this PDF prints VERSION 1.20 and copyright through 2026, unlike chapter 8's 1.10 footer; the edition field records the printed 1.20.

Ticket or nice assignment is the unresolved policy problem; per-tenant weights require an authority that sets and audits them, not self-service inflation by the tenant.
Proportional guarantees only bind when runnable demand exceeds capacity; state whether a capacity model assumes reserved shares or work-conserving sharing.

coverage: All 296 lines / 13 pages; sections 10.1-10.7, References, Homework (Simulation); figures 10.1-10.3 (two architecture diagrams, one code listing), unnumbered queue/timeline diagrams, one aside, two footnotes, nine homework questions; raster figures not visually inspected
figures: Figure 10.1: Single CPU With Cache (architecture diagram, text labels only)
Figure 10.2: Two CPUs With Caches Sharing Memory (architecture diagram, text labels only)
Figure 10.3: Simple List Delete Code (code listing, lines 64-108)
Unnumbered queue diagrams: five jobs on four CPUs, and Q0/Q1 assignments (text-rendered)
Unnumbered scheduling timelines: SQMS rotation, MQMS round robin, post-completion imbalance, migration sequence (text-rendered)
notes: The chapter traces multiprocessor ubiquity to power constraints that slowed single-core gains, then states the scheduling problem rather than assuming parallelism is free (source claim, introduction).
Coherence is assigned to hardware via bus snooping; the text notes that write-back caches complicate invalidation but does not derive a protocol (source claim, §10.1).
A coherent shared memory still permits the Figure 10.3 list race, so the chapter treats locks as a correctness requirement and only then raises their performance cost (source claim, §10.2).
Cache affinity is explicitly a performance heuristic: correct execution on a different CPU is preserved, but warm cache and TLB state are lost (source claim, §10.3).
SQMS is characterized as easy to retrofit and load-balanced by construction, with a single lock as the scaling bottleneck and cross-CPU job motion as the affinity cost (source claim, §10.4).
The MQMS examples show imbalance appearing even with equal initial queue lengths: after C exits, A receives twice the CPU of B and D, and after A and C exit one CPU has no work (source claim, §10.5).
Work stealing is presented with an unresolved polling-frequency trade-off; the chapter offers no threshold, measurement, or proof of convergence (source claim, §10.5).

Linux's O(1)/CFS (multi-queue) and BFS (single-queue) are cited as coexisting designs, which supports the inference that queue topology alone does not determine scheduler suitability (source claim plus inference, §10.6).
The closing warning that small code changes produce large behavioral differences is a design caution, not an empirical finding; the chapter reports no measurements of its own (inference, §10.7).

The homework asks readers to predict and then verify warm-cache speedup, affinity pinning, and super-linear speedup with multi.py; no simulator results are included in the text (source claim, Homework).

tycho_candidates.candidate: Add a single global run-queue lock as a concrete contention mechanism: it bounds scheduling scalability even when total CPU capacity is sufficient, and lock alternatives have their own scaling limits.
Use a shared list pop as a compact worked example that cache coherence does not enforce compound invariants; a mutex restores correctness at the cost of serializing the critical section.

Contrast one central work queue with per-worker queues: per-worker ownership improves locality and removes a global lock, but static assignment creates idle capacity and unequal shares unless work migrates.
Treat repeated job migration as control-loop churn: require a minimum imbalance threshold and residency interval before moving work, otherwise balancing overhead can cancel the capacity it seeks.

Source claim: binary buddy allocation splits power-of-two blocks and coalesces recursively, bounding coalescing work at the cost of rounding every request up to a power of two.

notes: Source claim: the TLB is a hardware cache of virtual-to-physical translations inside the MMU; a hit avoids the page-table memory reference, which the chapter says is what makes paging practical.
Source claim: a TLB miss costs an extra memory reference (more with multi-level tables), so hit rate depends on spatial and temporal locality, which are program properties rather than laws.

Source claim: the ten-integer array walk on 16-byte pages produces miss, hit, hit, miss, hit, hit, hit, miss, hit, hit (70% hits), i.e. one miss per page touched; larger pages would reduce misses further.

Source claim: hardware-managed TLBs (x86, CR3) walk a fixed page-table format, while software-managed TLBs (MIPS, SPARC v9) trap; the trap must resume the faulting instruction and avoid recursive misses via wired or unmapped handler entries.
Source claim: TLB valid bits mean entry occupancy, not page allocation; flushing sets them to zero, while ASIDs (8-bit versus 32-bit PIDs) let entries survive a context switch.
Source claim: LRU replacement is pessimal for a cyclic working set of n+1 pages with n TLB entries, whereas random eviction degrades more gracefully.
Source claim: the MIPS R4000 entry has a 19-bit user VPN, 24-bit PFN (64GB), global bit, 8-bit ASID, dirty/valid bits, page mask and wired entries; TLBP, TLBR, TLBWI and TLBWR must be privileged.

Source claim: TLB coverage, the set of pages reachable through the TLB, is the practical limit; once a working set exceeds it, misses dominate and large pages are the usual mitigation (for example in database systems).

Inference: TLB behavior is a hidden nonlinearity in end-to-end latency, so context pinning, warm-up and anti-dead-code-elimination controls are validity requirements for such measurements.
